newsitem.title: JAPAN: Romanian president confident of 1999 NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Romanian president confident of 1999 NATO entry.

text.p: Romanian President Emil Constantinescu said on Tuesday he was confident his country would be admitted to NATO membership when the alliance takes up the issue again in two year's time.

"U.S. President Bill Clinton told me that Romania is one of the top candidates.... That we will be able to join (NATO) in 1999 if we continue the current democratic process," Constantinescu told a news conference in Tokyo.

Constantinescu, in Japan since Sunday for a five-day visit, was referring to a meeting between him and the U.S. president, who made a brief stopover at Bucharest last week after a North Atlantic Treaty Organisation summit in Madrid.
At American insistence, only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic were invited to start talks on joining the alliance. Romania and Slovenia were named as prime candidates for future expansion.
During the news conference, Constantinescu gave an upbeat review of Romania's economic recovery and said his government was committed to continuing reforms.
"Our people want economic reform...and we pledge to continue the reforms," Constantinescu said.

Constantinescu said Romania was now a stable and reliable country in which to invest. He believed his talks in Tokyo so far had succeeded in persuading Japanese businessmen to invest in the former communist nation.
"I explained various projects in our country to our Japanese partners, and in my opinion, I think they are interested in investing," Constantinescu said.
Constantinescu said it was a sign of new ties that Japan has agreed to provide its first ever government-to-government loans to Romania.

The loans, agreed in a meeting between Constantinescu and Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda on Monday, are also the first such loans extended by Japan to a former East European communist nation.

The approximately 22 billion yen ($192 million) in loans was for infrastructure projects, with 12.8 billion yen ($112 million) for developing port facilities and 9.19 billion yen ($80.6 million) for building roads.

Romania's reformist government, which took power last November after seven years of leftist rule, has been scrambling to meet reform targets and secure the confidence of Western lenders and investors.
